# Part I: The ADNI Study (15 min)

## What is ADNI? (Slide 8)

**Key points**:

- Emphasize ADNI as the "gold standard" for AD research data
- Started 2004 under Michael Weiner (UCSF) and Leon Thal (UCSD)
- Public-private partnership model
- Data freely available (with DUA)

**Discussion prompt**: "How many of you have heard of ADNI before?"

## ADNI Study Design (Slide 9)

**Key points**:

- Walk through each phase and its focus
- Highlight the evolution: ADNI-1 established methods, later phases added
  biomarkers
- ADNI-4 focuses on diversity and novel digital biomarkers
- Total N = 3,032 is substantial for AD research

**Anticipated question**: "Why so many phases?"
**Answer**: Science evolves; new biomarkers (tau PET) and populations (diverse
recruitment) require new cohorts.

## Diagnostic Groups (Slide 10)

**Key points**:

- CN = Cognitively Normal (healthy controls)
- EMCI vs LMCI distinction based on Logical Memory II scores
- Emphasize that ADNI uses specific, operationalized criteria

**Teaching tip**: Draw the progression on board: CN → EMCI → LMCI → Dementia

## The alzverse (Slides 11-12)

**Key points**:

- NEW in 2026: ADNIMERGE2 replaces original ADNIMERGE
- Emphasize reproducibility benefits: vignettes, ADaM format
- Show GitHub documentation links
- Mention ~250 citations for original package

**Anticipated question**: "Can I still use the old ADNIMERGE?"
**Answer**: Yes, but ADNIMERGE2 has updated data and better documentation.
Recommend using ADNIMERGE2 for new projects.

## ADNI Baseline Characteristics (Slide 14)

**Key points**:

- 44% MCI at baseline - this is our target population
- Note diversity improvements in recent phases (ADNI-4: 35% Black/AA)
- Mean age ~72 years, well-educated sample (16 years)

**Discussion**: "What are limitations of this sample for generalizability?"


# Part II: Understanding MCI (10 min)

## MCI Definition (Slide 17)

**Key points**:

- Petersen criteria are the standard
- Emphasize: NOT demented, but NOT normal
- Subjective complaint + objective impairment
- ADLs preserved (distinguishes from dementia)

**Teaching tip**: Ask students to articulate why each criterion matters.

## MCI Subtypes (Slide 18)

**Key points**:

- Amnestic vs non-amnestic: memory primary or not
- Single vs multi-domain: how many cognitive areas affected
- ADNI focuses on amnestic MCI (highest AD risk)

## The Clinical Problem (Slide 19)

**Key points**:

- THIS IS THE MOTIVATION for the project
- Not all MCI converts - only 10-15% annually
- Clinical need: who will progress vs remain stable?
- Applications: treatment planning, trial enrollment, counseling

**Anticipated question**: "Why not just wait and see?"
**Answer**: Early intervention may be more effective; patients/families want
to plan; clinical trials need enriched populations.

## MCI to AD Conversion Rates (Slide 20)

**Key points**:

- From Grassi: 36% converted over 3 years
- This is the outcome students will predict
- Emphasize binary classification: converter vs stable


# Part III: Project 2 Hypothesis (10 min)

## Grassi et al. Study (Slide 22)

**Key points**:

- This paper defines the student project
- "Clinically translatable" = uses only standard clinical measures
- No imaging, no genetics (intentionally)
- Goal: practical tool for community clinics

**Read the abstract aloud** or have students read key sentences.

## Study Design (Slide 23)

**Key points**:

- N = 550 MCI subjects
- Baseline only (no longitudinal features)
- 3-year follow-up window
- Site-independent split is critical for generalization

## Key Results (Slide 24)

**Key points**:

- AUROC 0.88 is excellent for clinical prediction
- Sensitivity 77.7%: catches most converters
- Specificity 79.9%: few false alarms
- PPV/NPV are clinically meaningful

**Teaching tip**: Have students interpret: "If you test positive, what's the
probability you'll actually convert?" (PPV = 71.9%)

## Table 2 Image (Slide 25)

**Key points**:

- Show the actual table from the paper
- This is what students should reproduce
- Compare converters vs stable on each variable
- Note which variables differ significantly

## Why This Approach? (Slide 26)

**Key points**:

- Clinical translatability is the key innovation
- Contrast with high-tech approaches (PET, CSF, genetics)
- Community clinics can use these measures
- Trade accuracy for accessibility


# Part IV: Key Predictors (15 min)

## Feature Categories (Slide 28)

**Key points**:

- Four categories: sociodemographic, clinical scales, neuropsych, MCI subtype
- Note what's EXCLUDED: imaging, genetics
- This is a deliberate choice for clinical applicability

## Sociodemographic Features (Slide 29)

**Key points**:

- Age, education, sex, marital status
- These are "free" - already collected in clinic
- Marital status may proxy for social support/cognitive reserve

## Clinical Scales (Slide 30)

**Key points**:

- CDR-SB: Clinical Dementia Rating - Sum of Boxes
  - Clinician-rated based on interview
  - 6 domains, 0-18 scale
- FAQ: Functional Activities Questionnaire
  - Informant-rated
  - Instrumental ADLs

**Teaching tip**: Show example CDR-SB items if time permits.

## Neuropsychological Tests (Slide 31)

**Key points**:

- Walk through each test briefly
- MMSE: screening, ceiling effects in MCI
- ADAS-Cog: more detailed, designed for AD trials
- RAVLT: verbal memory, very sensitive to AD
- LDELTOTAL: Logical Memory delayed recall
- TMTB: executive function, processing speed

## ADAS-Cog Detail (Slide 32)

**Key points**:

- ADAS11 vs ADAS13: 13 adds delayed recall + cancellation
- ADAS13 is more sensitive to change
- Higher scores = worse performance (counterintuitive)

## RAVLT Detail (Slide 33)

**Key points**:

- 15-word list, 5 learning trials
- Interference list, then recall
- 30-minute delayed recall
- Derived scores: immediate, learning, forgetting

**Teaching tip**: Demonstrate briefly: "I'll read 15 words, you try to
remember as many as possible..."

## Feature Importance (Slide 34)

**Key points**:

- ADAS13 most important overall
- CDR-SB and FAQ: clinical staging
- RAVLT forgetting: memory retention is key
- MMSE less important than expected (ceiling effects)

**Discussion**: "Why might memory retention be more predictive than learning?"


# Part V: Machine Learning Methods (10 min)

## Overview (Slide 36)

**Key points**:

- Ensemble of 13 algorithms
- No single best algorithm
- Weighted rank averaging for final prediction

## Individual Algorithms (Slide 37)

**Key points**:

- Walk through categories briefly
- Students don't need to implement all 13
- Project requires at least 3 different algorithms

## Random Forest Example (Slide 38)

**Key points**:

- Show code structure
- ntree, mtry parameters
- Variable importance output

**Note**: Students can use caret or tidymodels to simplify this.

## Cross-Validation Strategy (Slide 39)

**Key points**:

- Site-independent split is KEY
- This prevents "cheating" on generalization
- 5-fold CV within training set
- Held-out test set for final evaluation

**Anticipated question**: "Why site-independent?"
**Answer**: Sites have systematic differences (equipment, protocols, patient
populations). Testing on new sites simulates real deployment.

## Evaluation Metrics (Slides 40-41)

**Key points**:

- Define each metric clearly
- AUROC: overall discrimination
- Sensitivity/specificity: threshold-dependent
- ROC curve shows trade-off

# Troubleshooting Guide

## Common Issues

**"ADNI access is taking too long"**

- DUA approval can take 1-2 weeks
- Students should apply immediately
- Instructor can provide subset for initial exploration

**"ADNIMERGE2 won't install"**

- Check R version (needs 4.0+)
- Install dependencies first
- Try: `install.packages("ADNIMERGE2_x.x.x.tar.gz", repos = NULL,
  type = "source")`

**"Can't find MCI subjects"**

- Filter on DX_BL (baseline diagnosis)
- Use: `filter(DX_BL %in% c("EMCI", "LMCI"))`

**"How do I define converters?"**

- Any subsequent diagnosis of "Dementia"
- Use longitudinal DX variable, not just baseline

**"My AUROC is much lower than Grassi"**

- Check feature engineering
- Verify train/test split
- Consider different algorithms
- 0.70-0.80 is still acceptable for student project


# Anticipated Questions

**Q: Do we need to use all 13 algorithms like Grassi?**

A: No. Minimum 3 different algorithms required. Focus on understanding the
methods rather than replicating everything.

**Q: Can we include imaging or genetic features?**

A: For the core project, follow Grassi (clinical only). You may explore
imaging/genetics as an extension if time permits.

**Q: What if my results differ from Grassi?**

A: Expected! Different random seeds, slightly different cohort selection,
different software versions. Focus on methodology, not exact replication.

**Q: How do I handle missing data?**

A: Document your approach. Options: complete case analysis, imputation,
or exclude variables with high missingness. Justify your choice.

**Q: Can we work in groups?**

A: Analysis should be individual. You may discuss concepts and debug code
together, but each student submits their own work.
